p: A sarissa had two main parts, a long wooden shaft and a metal tip; some may also have had a metal butt at the other end, with which the weapon could be stood in the ground without damage to the shaft. Ash, which is long, flexible and light, and cornel wood, which is shorter but stronger, are the likeliest woods. It replaced the considerably shorter dory.

Ancient writers agree that its length set it apart, but not on the figure: Theophrastus, a contemporary of Alexander the Great, puts the longest at 12 cubits, and Polybius gives 16 cubits in the original design, reduced in practice to 14. In modern units this suggests about 5.8 m in Alexander's time and perhaps 6.3 m later.

The weapon needed both hands, so the phalangite carried only a smaller shield, the pelta, perhaps hung from a neck strap. On the march the sarissas were held upright; levelled for battle, fully five rows of points projected in front of the first rank, while the rear ranks held theirs angled upward, which also deflected arrows. A phalanx so formed was considered practically invulnerable from the front, but it turned with difficulty, and a soldier out of formation had to fall back on a sword or dagger.

Sarissa-armed phalanxes were vital in the early battles of Alexander, including the Battle of Gaugamela, though in his later campaigns he gradually reduced their importance. The surest way to beat such a phalanx was to break its formation or outflank it, as the Romans did at the Battle of Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE. A light cavalry unit of Alexander's army, the sarissophoroi, carried somewhat shorter versions; Nicholas Victor Sekunda argues that the Macedonian cavalry spear is better classed as a xyston.

A leaf-shaped spearhead 51 cm long, found by Manolis Andronikos in a Macedonian tomb at Vergina, shaped much scholarship between 1970 and 2000, but more recent work doubts that it belonged to a sarissa; Sekunda favours a small diamond-shaped iron tip of about 13.5 cm. Earlier estimates put the weight at 5.5 to 6.5 kg, yet Peter Connolly reconstructed a pike 5.8 m long in cherry wood that weighed only 4.05 kg. Scholars also draw on later pikemen, such as the Swiss and the German Landsknecht: preserved English pikes are 5.6 to 5.9 m long, which suggests that the lengths reported for the Macedonian weapon were workable.

notes: The article writes 'Battle of Cynoscephalae (197 BC)'; given here as BCE.
Shield sizes are disputed in the article (60 cm, 45 cm, or 65-75 cm); I gave none.
Left out Machiavelli's 1521 comparison with the Swiss and Livy's passage on Pydna for length.
The wood of every shaft has rotted away, as the article says; lengths rest on ancient writers and reconstructions.
